claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE checkpoints without waiting for readers or writers, syncing the database file if all log frames were checkpointed.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE Checkpoint as many frames as possible without waiting for any database readers or writers to finish, then sync the database file if all frames in the log were checkpointed.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL waits until there is no writer and all readers use the most recent snapshot before checkpointing all frames and syncing the database file.
claims.quote: until there is no database writer and all readers are reading from the most recent database snapshot. It then checkpoints all frames in the log file and syncs the database file.

claims.text: After checkpointing, SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART waits until all readers use only the database file, ensuring the next writer restarts the WAL from the beginning.
claims.quote: after checkpointing the log file it blocks (calls the busy-handler callback ) until all readers are reading from the database file only. This ensures that the next writer will restart the log file from the beginning.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE performs SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART behavior and additionally truncates the log to zero bytes just before a successful return.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART with the addition that it also truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior to a successful return.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP obtains *pnLog and *pnCkpt status while checkpointing zero frames.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP This mode always checkpoints zero frames. The only reason to invoke a NOOP checkpoint is to access the values returned by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() via output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt.

claims.text: S2 specifies that pending SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART checkpoints, like SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL checkpoints, block new writer attempts without impeding readers.
claims.quote: Like SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL, this mode blocks new database writer attempts while it is pending, but does not impede readers.

claims.text: sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint(D,N) triggers a checkpoint after a transaction commits if its WAL contains at least N frames.
claims.quote: The sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint(D,N) is a wrapper around sqlite3_wal_hook() that causes any database on database connection D to automatically checkpoint after committing a transaction if there are N or more frames in the write-ahead log file.

claims.text: Passing N=0 or a negative N to sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint() disables automatic checkpoints.
claims.quote: Passing zero or a negative value as the N parameter disables automatic checkpoints entirely.

claims.text: Every new database connection defaults to automatic checkpointing with a threshold of 1000 or SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT pages.
claims.quote: Every new database connection defaults to having the auto-checkpoint enabled with a threshold of 1000 or SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT pages.

claims.text: Checkpoints initiated by sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint() are PASSIVE.
claims.quote: The wal_autocheckpoint pragma can be used to invoke this interface from SQL. Checkpoints initiated by this mechanism are PASSIVE .

claims.text: If another process is already running a checkpoint, failure to acquire the checkpoint lock returns SQLITE_BUSY without invoking the busy-handler.
claims.quote: If any other process is running a checkpoint operation at the same time, the lock cannot be obtained and SQLITE_BUSY is returned. Even if there is a busy-handler configured, it will not be invoked in this case.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE never invokes the busy-handler callback.
claims.quote: The busy-handler callback is never invoked in the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE mode. On the other hand, passive mode might leave the checkpoint unfinished if there are concurrent readers or writers.

claims.text: For SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL, SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART and SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE, a busy-handler return of 0 while waiting for the writer lock or readers causes fallback to SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE behavior.
claims.quote: If the busy-handler returns 0 before the writer lock is obtained or while waiting for database readers, the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE

claims.text: A checkpoint that falls back to SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE after busy-handler refusal returns SQLITE_BUSY.
claims.quote: the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE - checkpointing as many frames as possible without blocking any further. SQLITE_BUSY is returned in this case.

claims.text: If overlapping readers always leave at least one reader active, checkpoints cannot complete and the WAL grows without bound.
claims.quote: However, if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers and there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.

claims.text: Checkpoint starvation can be avoided by arranging reader gaps and attempting checkpoints during those gaps.
claims.quote: This scenario can be avoided by ensuring that there are "reader gaps": times when no processes are reading from the database and that checkpoints are attempted during those times.

claims.text: Default checkpointing runs in the thread executing the threshold-crossing COMMIT, making checkpoint-triggering COMMIT operations occasionally much slower.
claims.quote: same thread that does the COMMIT that pushes the WAL over its size limit. This has the effect of causing most COMMIT operations to be very fast but an occasional COMMIT (those that trigger a checkpoint) to be much slower.

claims.text: Infrequent checkpoints amortize checkpoint cost across more writes while allowing a larger WAL.
claims.quote: To maximize write performance, one wants to amortize the cost of each checkpoint over as many writes as possible, meaning that one wants to run checkpoints infrequently and let the WAL grow as large as possible before each checkpoint.

claims.text: A writer can rewind the WAL when all its contents have been transferred to the database and synced and no readers still use the WAL.
claims.quote: if the entire WAL has been transferred into the database and synced and if no readers are making use of the WAL, then the writer will rewind the WAL back to the beginning

claims.text: Checkpoints normally reuse the WAL from its beginning without truncation, with journal_size_limit identified as an exception.
claims.quote: The checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file (unless the journal_size_limit pragma is set). Instead, it merely causes SQLite to start overwriting the WAL file from the beginning.

claims.text: When pnLog is non-NULL and the checkpoint runs without an error on a WAL database, *pnLog reports the total number of log frames.
claims.quote: If pnLog is not NULL, then *pnLog is set to the total number of frames in the log file

claims.text: The *pnCkpt count includes frames checkpointed before the current call, rather than only frames checkpointed by that call.
claims.quote: If pnCkpt is not NULL,then *pnCkpt is set to the total number of checkpointed frames in the log file (including any that were already checkpointed before the function was called)

claims.text: If zDb names an attached database outside WAL mode, sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() returns SQLITE_OK and sets both frame counters to -1.
claims.quote: If database zDb is the name of an attached database that is not in WAL mode, SQLITE_OK is returned and both *pnLog and *pnCkpt set to -1.

claims.text: A checkpoint must stop when it reaches a WAL page past any current reader's end mark.
claims.quote: A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers, however the checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader.

claims.text: A partial checkpoint records its progress in the wal-index and resumes from that position on its next invocation.
claims.quote: The checkpoint remembers (in the wal-index) how far it got and will resume transferring content from the WAL to the database from where it left off on the next invocation.

claims.text: Checkpointing must sync the WAL before transferring its content into the database and sync the database before resetting the WAL.
claims.quote: The WAL must be synced to persistent storage prior to moving content from the WAL into the database and the database file must be synced prior to resetting the WAL.

claims.text: For WAL commits, PRAGMA synchronous=FULL syncs the WAL on every commit, whereas PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL omits that commit-time sync.
claims.quote: (Writers sync the WAL on every transaction commit if PRAGMA synchronous is set to FULL but omit this sync if PRAGMA synchronous is set to NORMAL.)

claims.text: Omitting synchronization of WAL content to disk sacrifices durability following a power loss or hard reboot.
claims.quote: Further, syncing the content to the disk is not required, as long as the application is willing to sacrifice durability following a power loss or hard reboot.

claims.text: A reader's end mark remains unchanged throughout its transaction, preserving a single point-in-time view.
claims.quote: But for any particular reader, the end mark is unchanged for the duration of the transaction, thus ensuring that a single read transaction only sees the database content as it existed at a single point in time.

claims.text: Registering a sqlite3_wal_hook() callback disables automatic checkpointing configured by sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint().
claims.quote: The callback registered by this function replaces any existing callback registered using sqlite3_wal_hook() . Likewise, registering a callback using sqlite3_wal_hook() disables the automatic checkpoint mechanism configured by this function.

claims.text: The WAL cannot be reset during a write transaction, so a large write transaction can produce a large WAL.
claims.quote: which means the WAL file cannot be reset in the middle of a write transaction. So a large change to a large database might result in a large WAL file.

claims.text: A WAL-mode COMMIT occurs when a special commit record is appended to the WAL.
claims.quote: A COMMIT occurs when a special record indicating a commit is appended to the WAL.

claims.text: The wal-index's shared-memory requirement confines readers to the same machine and prevents this WAL implementation from working on a network filesystem.
claims.quote: the use of shared memory means that all readers must exist on the same machine. This is why the write-ahead log implementation will not work on a network filesystem.

claims.text: If zDb is NULL or an empty string, sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() attempts the operation on every WAL database attached to the connection.
claims.quote: If parameter zDb is NULL or points to a zero length string, then the specified operation is attempted on all WAL databases attached to database connection db.

claims.text: When a checkpoint call targets all attached WAL databases, its *pnLog and *pnCkpt output values are undefined.
claims.quote: the specified operation is attempted on all WAL databases attached to database connection db. In this case the values written to output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt are undefined.

claims.text: After a crash or ROLLBACK, rollback-journal recovery restores the database's original state by replaying the journal's original content.
claims.quote: In the event of a crash or ROLLBACK , the original content contained in the rollback journal is played back into the database file to revert the database file to its original state.

limitations: SQLite, transactions and write-ahead logging are treated as existing coverage and omitted as candidates; novelty reflects narrower gaps relative to those three inventory entries.
R, U, N, I and V denote relevance, usefulness, novelty, interest and viability on 0–5 scales; CVS uses weights 0.25, 0.25, 0.20, 0.15 and 0.15, with a 3.20 threshold and the supplied hard gates.
Scores are bounded judgments from the supplied rubric and packet; no da-* activation or automated score verification was performed under the no-tools override.

All three sources share the sqlite.org origin, and several concepts have only one directly relevant page; RESEARCH indicates selection priority, not satisfaction of a full /dr independent-source floor.
No supplied evidence establishes frontier developments within the last 12–18 months, so no frontier candidates are manufactured; the SQLite 3.11.0 note dated 2016 is historical evidence.

S1's application-initiated mode summary lists PASSIVE, FULL and RESTART and later mentions RESET, while S2 explicitly defines TRUNCATE and NOOP as well; the packet provides no chronology explaining these differences.

S1 warns that RESTART and TRUNCATE might block readers, whereas S2 says RESTART does not impede readers and describes TRUNCATE as extending RESTART; the packet does not reconcile these descriptions, so the mode-specific claim is explicitly attributed to S2.
Parent and neighborhood assignments are analytical classifications grounded in the packet, not a taxonomy explicitly supplied by SQLite.
One bounded extraction pass is reported; new_information_rate equals new unique claims divided by cumulative claims after that pass, and no depth or frontier saturation is asserted.
